newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Justice Minister resigns for campaign job.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Justice Minister resigns for campaign job.

text.p: Colombia's Justice Minister, an outspoken supporter of efforts to lift the country's ban on extradition, resigned on Monday in a move that stripped President Ernesto Samper of one of his top and most respected aides.

Carlos Medellin, who has won high marks from Washington for his role in pushing tough anti-drug laws through Congress, told a news conference he was stepping down to go to work on the presidential campaign of Carlos Lleras de la Fuente.
"My future work is alongside Carlos Lleras," Medellin said.

Lleras, the son of a former president of the same name, resigned as Colombia's ambassador to Washington last year amid the scandal over charges Samper used drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign. He has openly criticised Samper since leaving the embassy post.
Lleras is one of the first "pre-candidates" to announce his intention to stand in presidential elections set for May 1998, but recent public opinion polls indicate he has little grassroots support.

Samper responded to Medellin's resignation in a letter made public late on Monday by saying he regretted the move but accepted it nonetheless. He also announced that he had named Alma Beatriz Rengifo de Estrada, a little known lawyer who has served until now as his special legal counsellor, to fill the post that Medellin took up just last year.

Medellin -- a proponent of cracking down on Colombia's criminal drug gangs -- said in his resignation letter to Samper that "giant steps" had been taken on his watch to tighten the penalties for drug trafficking.

These include a new asset-forfeiture law, allowing the government to seize billions of dollars in wealth from convicted traffickers, and legislation approved in February that nearly triples the maximum prison term for drug-related offences.
The measures, according to Medellin's letter, put Colombia "in the vanguard of the fight against drug trafficking and organised crime."
Medellin heaped praise on Samper in his resignation letter, lauding his "admirable character" and "patriotic commitment to building a dignified, just and democratic Colombia."
In what government sources said was an apparent typographical error, the letter, dated April 17, also referred to Samper's "special way of building each moment of difficulty," however.

Samper announced earlier this month, at the urging of Medellin and intense U.S. pressure, that he would soon propose legislation aimed at lifting the constitutional ban on extradition of drug lords and other criminals introduced by Colombia's constituent assembly in 1991.

Political analysts and diplomats say the government faces a long, uphill battle to win approval of the legislation, since most Colombians oppose extradition and drug barons have demonstrated an uncanny ability to influence many legislators in the past.
U.S. officials have said repeatedly that detention in a secure facility in the United States is what Colombia's powerful drug lords fear the most.
